title: Points Inside a Viewing Cone
statement:
You stand at the grid point at = [x, y] and can turn on the spot, but not move. Your view is a cone fov degrees wide: once you pick a facing direction, you see every point whose direction from you lies within that cone, edges included.

You get a list of integer points; several may share a position. Points never block each other. A point at your own position is always seen, whatever way you face.

Return the largest number of points you can see at once by choosing the best direction.

examples.why: Seen from (1, 1), the first point lies due east (0°) and the second due north (90°). A 90° cone holds both, edges included. The third is at about 198°.
The first two points are at about 354° and 6°. The best cone wraps across 0°, which a window over sorted angles misses unless the angles are allowed to go around the circle.
The point at your feet always counts. The other two are opposite each other, so a narrow cone sees one of them.

constraints: −100 ≤ x, y ≤ 100 for every point and for at
hints: Only the direction to each point matters, not its distance. Turn each point into one angle around you.
After sorting the angles, a cone is a range of consecutive angles whose first and last differ by at most fov. That is a sliding window, except that the circle wraps around at 360°.
Handle the wrap by appending every angle again plus 360 and sliding over the doubled list. Count points sitting exactly at your position separately and add them at the end.

explain.intuition:
Distance is irrelevant, so each point becomes a single angle, atan2(dy, dx) converted to degrees in [0, 360). The question is then: what is the largest group of angles that fits in an arc of width fov? With sorted angles, that is the longest window whose first and last value differ by at most fov, a plain sliding window.

The only twist is the circle. An arc can run from 350° past 0° to 10°. Copying the sorted list with 360 added to each angle turns the circle into a line twice as long, and every arc becomes a contiguous window on it. Points at your own position have no angle at all; count them separately and add them to the best window.
steps: For each point, compute dx, dy from at. If both are 0, increase here; otherwise store its angle in degrees, shifted into [0, 360).
Sort the angles and append each angle + 360 to the end.
Slide a window: for each right end, move the left end forward while the span exceeds fov (with a tiny tolerance for floating-point error). Track the largest window size.
pitfalls: Ignoring the wrap-around at 0°. The second example needs a cone that spans 354° to 6°.
Comparing floating-point angles exactly. A point at exactly 90° may compute as 90.00000000000001; use a small tolerance like 1e-9.
Giving points at your own position an angle. atan2(0, 0) is 0, which would put them in some windows and not others.

solutions.title: Try every point as the cone's edge
solutions.idea: Some best cone starts exactly at a point's angle. For each angle, count the angles within fov degrees counterclockwise of it.

solutions.title: Sorted angles, doubled, sliding window
solutions.idea: Sort the angles, append each one plus 360 to unroll the circle, and find the widest window spanning at most fov degrees.

followups: Points now block the ones directly behind them on the same ray. How do you count only the nearest point per direction?
Answer many different fov values for the same points and position. What can you precompute?
